title: Validity of the outside median conduction study
clarityIssues: The task asks whether a conduction result supports an unspecified intervention. Confirming the validity of a measurement and establishing an indication for treatment are different decisions; name which decision is being tested.
This singleton supplies its own history and task. No missing earlier answer is needed.

cues.phrase: no same-distance control-nerve comparison was recorded
cues.why: A named omission points directly to the only option containing 'control-nerve'; a reader can repair the stated omission without interpreting the sensory distribution.

cues.phrase: Temperature-controlled median and control-nerve conduction studies
cues.why: Only this label advertises correction of both conspicuous acquisition details. The other tests are not parallel alternatives for verifying an existing conduction measurement.

cues.phrase: the actual acquisition sheet rather than just the outside report's conclusion
cues.why: This pre-answer editorial framing tells the learner to distrust the conclusion and choose technical reacquisition.

fairness: Controlled repeat conduction testing is defensible for the narrow measurement-validity question. No confident clinical error is identified in that choice.

Ultrasound can contribute to assessment of median neuropathy, but the lead-in preselects physiological-result validation and thereby handicaps that option. This is a task-construction problem rather than evidence that ultrasound has no clinical role.
The exact temperature and acquisition claims were not independently source-verified in this offline review. No new numerical threshold is asserted.
The tested acquisition detail is more specialized than the high-yield general-surgery objective of localizing median neuropathy and recognizing consequential motor loss.
suggestions: Choose a concrete decision: validation of a supplied physiological study, or selection of the next investigation for unresolved symptoms. Do not conflate it with eligibility for an unspecified intervention.

If retaining study validity, show a compact acquisition/result record and offer comparably specific study strategies; remove the named-omission and report-distrust commentary while retaining necessary technical facts.

Make the clinical localization change which technical or diagnostic plan is appropriate. Otherwise classify this as a focused technical item requiring explicit acceptance, not a difficult two-step resident item.

title: Progressive thenar motor loss despite sensory improvement
fairness: Hand-surgical assessment for carpal tunnel release is the single best offered referral: the motor examination and selective distal physiology localize the consequential deficit, and progressive weakness despite sensory benefit changes the escalation decision.

The old cervical abnormality and improved tingling are credible competing considerations. Normal sampled proximal recruitment does not exclude every root disorder; the explanation appropriately avoids that claim.

Palmar abduction is described explicitly, avoiding confusion with thumb extension. The independent case contains the relevant injection response, motor course and studies, so 'At a later hand review' does not require a preceding node.
Entrapment localization and escalation for progressive motor loss are high-yield principles. Difficulty is a qualitative prediction, not measured exam performance.
suggestions: Optional tightening: let the raw sensory and motor trends establish their divergence instead of announcing it in the current update.
Keep the distinction between referral for surgical assessment and an unconditional instruction to operate. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

title: Broader neurological findings after a focal elbow diagnosis
clarityIssues: The clinical chronology is understandable and self-contained. The main defect is weak discrimination, not ambiguous anatomy.

cues.phrase: extended beyond the initially investigated right elbow territory
cues.why: The update states the localization mismatch that the resident should infer.

Both distractors explicitly image only the right upper limb. Together with walking difficulty, this permits a broad-versus-local elimination strategy without knowing the specific neurological syndrome.

cues.phrase: Both knee reflexes are brisk with sustained ankle clonus
cues.why: This is necessary clinical information, not an inappropriate fact to conceal. However, with two unilateral arm-imaging distractors it reduces the item to familiar cord-pattern recognition rather than a second consequential decision.

fairness: Cervical spine MRI is the defensible best answer. Neither a unilateral plexus lesion nor elbow pathology explains the supplied bilateral hand and lower-limb findings.
There is no confident clinical inaccuracy. The explanation correctly permits a true focal elbow lesion to coexist with a broader disorder.

Cervical myelopathy recognition is high yield, but naming the imaging study after this classic pattern is not independently difficult application. The initial elbow record is not needed to choose the key from these options.
suggestions: Remove the authored 'extended beyond' interpretation and retain the examination observations.

Use a credible competing evaluation at the same neurological decision stage, with supported findings that genuinely determine the next action; do not merely substitute another implausible unilateral image.
Alternatively request explicit acceptance as an easy safety/localization item. Preserve clonus and gait findings rather than making an urgent condition harder by concealing them.

title: Motor deterioration with bilateral ulnar nerve mobility
clarityIssues: 'Refer for bilateral cubital-tunnel surgical assessment' describes assessment, not bilateral surgery. The explanation treats it as equivalent escalation on both sides, which the option does not necessarily require.
The standalone case otherwise supplies the earlier protective care, bilateral examination and studies.

cues.phrase: Left hand strength, sensation and conduction remain normal
cues.why: This explicitly clears every offered basis for treating the left side; the additional statement that the left arm has no symptoms repeats the elimination of the bilateral distractor.

cues.phrase: the tingling has improved but right-hand motor function has deteriorated
cues.why: The current update supplies the interpretation that defeats continued conservative symptom care before the learner reads the findings.

cues.phrase: Refer for bilateral cubital-tunnel surgical assessment
cues.why: Against a fully normal left examination, this is a conspicuous overtreatment foil rather than a close competing clinical decision.

fairness: Right-sided surgical assessment is defensible for progressive objective motor loss with concordant physiology despite less tingling.

Bilateral nerve mobility does not establish bilateral symptomatic neuropathy. However, assessing both elbows at a specialist visit is not itself the same as recommending treatment of an asymptomatic elbow; the options need a sharper, nonoverlapping action distinction.
The core escalation principle is high yield. The current side-selection component is too explicitly resolved to supply a second consequential inference.
suggestions: Compare distinct care plans with comparable scope, separating which side warrants intervention from which sides may be examined during assessment.
Retain clinically necessary contralateral findings but remove the duplicate absence-of-symptoms statement and the interpretive update.

Either make the bilateral structural finding consequential to a genuinely unresolved decision or omit it and acknowledge that the remaining escalation item is straightforward. Do not introduce an unsupported decompression-versus-transposition key.

title: Recovery after postoperative trapezius dysfunction
clarityIssues: The explanation includes author workflow language: 'Melissa must confirm this exact pathway'. Clinical-review status belongs outside learner-facing teaching.
There is no missing earlier node, but the exact extent of residual functional disability and the current specialist follow-up plan are not described.

cues.phrase: With supervised rehabilitation, overhead reach and resisted shrug have improved on successive examinations
cues.why: The only conservative option repeats 'supervised' and 'rehabilitation'; two escalating surgical pathways oppose an explicitly successful current treatment.

cues.phrase: new voluntary motor units with greater recruitment
cues.why: This reinforces the same recovery direction. Deleting this technical row still leaves continued rehabilitation as the obvious answer, so it does not earn a second scored inference.

fairness: Continued rehabilitation and reassessment is plausible with improving function and recruitment. No definite clinical error is established by this offline review.

Uncertainty: improvement does not by itself settle every surgical-referral question after an iatrogenic accessory-nerve injury. The extent and course of recovery and the existing specialist plan matter; the stem should not teach that any improvement categorically excludes exploration assessment.

Accessory-nerve injury after posterior-triangle surgery is high yield. That localization is unnecessary for choosing the uniquely conservative option here, and the tendon-transfer alternative is a remote-stage competitor.
suggestions: Test a meaningful residual decision using the actual function attempted and a clinically supported recovery course, rather than persistent appearance versus two premature operations.
Clarify the existing peripheral-nerve follow-up and relevant disability without inventing a repair deadline or numerical recovery threshold.
Replace author-review commentary with concise clinical feedback, and retain needs_clinician_review outside the learner text.

title: Joint sampling and antibiotic sequence in a stable patient
fairness: Aspirating the knee before empiric antibiotics is the single best offered sequence for this concerning native-joint presentation with preserved systemic physiology and blood cultures already collected.

The meaningful second decision is treatment order: antibiotics are appropriate, but the physiological state determines whether obtaining the joint specimen first is reasonable. The antibiotic-first option is a credible sequencing error rather than an absurd treatment.

Normal blood pressure, mentation and perfusion are necessary decision information, not gratuitous distractor exclusions. The explanation appropriately changes the priority when sepsis makes delay unsafe.

The retrospective clinic frame, age/sex, knee findings and task stand alone. The phrase 'next dated' is unnecessary continuity language but does not omit information needed to answer. No exact waiting interval is taught.
suggestions: Optional tightening: replace the generic 'next dated outside-hospital record' update with a short initial-assessment label.
Preserve the stability-dependent sequence and avoid expanding the feedback into permission to delay antibiotics for an unspecified prolonged period. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

title: Aspirate compartment and repeat knee access route
clarityIssues: The exhibit provides prose about procedure images, not an image. 'The outside team has the procedure images' and 'The images show what was sampled' should identify these as reported observations if no actual image is intended.

The update already decides that another local sample is needed, and the task narrows the answer to an aspiration route. The resident is not asked to decide whether the crystal-containing specimen resolves the joint question.
The singleton contains the sample result, sampled location and current examination; there is no dependence on the prior aspiration node.

cues.phrase: skin over the lateral suprapatellar recess is intact
cues.why: This uniquely repeats the location in the key, while both distractors are anterior entries and the preceding sentence explicitly places redness and a collection anteriorly. The option set can be solved as an intact-versus-inflamed-route match.

cues.phrase: must decide how to obtain the next local sample
cues.why: This announces the sampling decision instead of allowing specimen provenance to change whether and what to sample.

fairness: The lateral suprapatellar joint route is the best offered plan. Sampling the superficial pocket does not establish the contents of a separate joint effusion, and traversing the inflamed collection is an avoidable concern.
No confident clinical error is identified. The crystal finding and negative Gram stain do not settle the joint question, as the explanation correctly states.

The provenance and access principles are high yield, but deleting the crystal report and first-sample narrative still leaves the same route selected from the current effusion and skin findings. The apparent two-step construction collapses in this option set.
suggestions: Use a neutral next-management task so interpretation of the specimen location determines the next plan before access-route selection is applied.
Offer credible plans at that same decision stage; do not make two choices repeat the one explicitly inflamed entry location.

Keep necessary skin and compartment observations. Repair the task/options rather than conceal safety information. Label the exhibit as a procedure report or provide the intended usable teaching image.

title: Prioritizing limited synovial fluid after a positive PCR

cues.phrase: the original culture had not produced an isolate
cues.why: The stem identifies the unfinished investigation, and the first option directly supplies that investigation. This is legitimate microbiological context but also an obvious completion cue in this otherwise single-rule item.

fairness: Bacterial culture is the defensible best priority among the requested analyses when the limited new specimen must support unresolved microbiology. PCR detection does not itself provide a viable isolate for standard susceptibility testing.
The choices are parallel, specific and not length or absolute outliers. No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified.

The limited-volume prioritization rule already chooses culture without the PCR row. The molecular result provides a potential misconception but does not force a second consequential application in the current stem.

The case is self-contained. Preserving microbiological diagnosis in suspected joint infection is high yield; the precise assay-allocation fact is a narrower teaching point. This is not a statistics item and does not inherit the single-skill exception.
suggestions: Either obtain explicit acceptance for a focused foundational specimen-priority item, or redesign the sample-allocation decision so existing usable specimens/results genuinely change what must be secured next.

For a harder revision, supply a concise actual specimen inventory and a consequential unresolved clinical need, with adequately supported alternatives. Do not invent laboratory minimum volumes or unsupported susceptibility capabilities.

title: Persistent knee infection despite active antibiotics
fairness: Repeat arthroscopic knee debridement is the best offered next treatment: persistent purulence, reaccumulation and worsening motion pain indicate unresolved local infection despite an active delivered antibiotic regimen.

The resident must distinguish failed source control from antimicrobial inadequacy before selecting the treatment. Broader antibiotics are a credible error when inflammatory findings worsen; susceptibility and administration records are necessary to rank that alternative.
The explanation correctly avoids making an isolated CRP increase an operative threshold. No confident clinical inaccuracy or second equally defensible best answer is apparent among these choices.

Earlier washout, current findings and treatment verification are fully restated in the singleton. This is a high-yield surgical source-control decision, not a requirement to remember an earlier answer.
suggestions: Preserve the combination of worsening local findings and verified active treatment. Do not simplify the trigger to CRP alone.
Optional precision: align the explanation's 'debridement assessment' language with whether the task scores referral or the next operative treatment. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

title: Postoperative calf pain and progressive motor deficit

cues.phrase: The calf became swollen and firm, and passive toe movement markedly increased pain
cues.why: These are important danger signs that must remain visible. With a matching calf-compartment assessment and two tests that do not address the acute pressure problem, they produce classic safety recognition rather than difficult two-step reasoning.

cues.phrase: Immediate surgical assessment of calf compartments
cues.why: This is the only bedside surgical assessment among two instrumented investigations. The scope/type difference reinforces the obvious urgent-recognition key.

fairness: Immediate surgical compartment assessment is the single defensible best answer. Palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome, and the initial return of movement makes simply attributing the subsequent deterioration to an ongoing block inappropriate.
No confident clinical error is identified. The explanation reasonably reserves pressure measurement for situations in which it assists assessment rather than requiring it before action.
The block chronology defeats an alternative that is not actually offered. Removing it leaves the same key from the local signs; it does not create a second consequential decision.

The retrospective setting and all immediate findings are supplied within this singleton, including the repeat washout. Compartment syndrome is high yield and may warrant an explicitly accepted easy safety exception.
suggestions: Seek explicit independent/manager acceptance as a safety-recognition item and label its intended ease honestly, or develop a separate supported decision after recognition with genuinely plausible competing actions.

Do not hide pain with passive movement, progression, or other urgent findings to manufacture difficulty. Do not add a new pressure cutoff or allow testing to delay a clearly indicated surgical response.

title: Imaging persistent inflammatory back pain
fairness: Contrast-enhanced lumbar MRI is the best offered investigation for persistent focal pain with inflammatory evidence and no adequate cross-sectional assessment. Afebrile status and degenerative radiographs do not settle the cause.

No confident clinical inaccuracy or strong nonmedical wording shortcut is identified. The elevated CRP is nonspecific; the explanation appropriately supports investigation rather than claiming a proven infection.

The task already requires another spine study, so the resident never has to reject stopping at degenerative disease. Selecting MRI from CT and bone scan is a conventional modality rule, not two consequential steps.
The case stands alone, and recognizing spinal-infection red flags is high yield. The current options do not meaningfully test the proposed error of attributing everything to degeneration.
suggestions: Either retain this as an explicitly accepted basic imaging/red-flag item or ask a neutral next-evaluation decision in which the inflammatory course actually changes management.

For a resident-level revision, use a credible competing next step and a relevant, supported acquisition or patient constraint that changes the choice. Avoid decorative extra values and unsupported contraindications.

title: Spinal tissue acquisition and the antibiotic-starting boundary
clarityIssues: The task is explicit about specimen acquisition versus final culture results, so that ambiguity is repaired. However, it now asserts a clinically consequential treatment boundary that requires exact confirmation.
The update and microbiology row repeat that no antimicrobials have been administered. The standalone case otherwise provides the relevant MRI, cultures, stability and neurological observations.
fairness: Image-guided disc/endplate sampling before empiric antibiotics is the best of the four offered sequences in this untreated, stable patient with negative blood cultures and no stated decompression or stabilization indication.

The option matrix is balanced: each sampling route and treatment order occurs twice. There is no majority-component convergence shortcut. Route selection and protection of diagnostic yield are two consequential decisions.

Unresolved clinical boundary, not a confirmed error: the lead-in and explanation endorse beginning empiric therapy after specimen acquisition rather than awaiting microbiological diagnosis. Guidance for stable native vertebral osteomyelitis may frame withholding treatment until microbiological diagnosis is established. This offline review cannot establish when the post-acquisition empiric plan is preferred for this exact patient; merely defining the phrase does not resolve that ranking.

This is a high-yield infection-workup principle, but a best-of-offered answer should not silently imply that a potentially defensible culture-directed waiting plan is inappropriate. No drug regimen or numerical treatment interval is inferred.
suggestions: Have the named clinician confirm the exact acquisition-versus-microbiological-diagnosis treatment boundary against the permitted evidence before retaining the stated post-biopsy rule.

If that boundary remains unresolved, restrict the scored task to the immediate tissue-acquisition route and pre-acquisition antibiotic decision, without promising routine empiric treatment immediately afterward.

Alternatively provide supported patient-specific information that determines why post-acquisition empiric treatment is preferred over awaiting an etiologic result. Do not invent a deterioration risk or delay threshold.

title: Worsening bony MRI appearance during clinical improvement
fairness: Continuing planned pathogen-directed treatment is the single best offered response to improving pain, walking tolerance and inflammatory markers without a new neural or mechanical complication.

The worsening endplate/disc appearance supplies real conflicting evidence. Interpreting that discordance and then choosing whether to escalate treatment are consequential steps; antibiotic broadening and surgery represent recognizable overreactions to imaging.

The negative neurological and structural observations establish why continued treatment is reasonable. They are necessary safety information rather than a reason to remove those alternatives from all future cases.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation does not endorse stopping therapy or require radiographic normalization. The established diagnosis and complete course are included in the singleton. Interpreting response and source-control indications is high yield.
suggestions: Preserve the distinction between bony imaging evolution and new epidural, neural or mechanical complications. Do not generalize this answer to every worsening MRI during infection.
Optional tightening: remove the generic 'next dated' update. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

title: Concordant infection at one spinal site and a distinct second lesion
fairness: Image-guided T8 lesion biopsy for culture and histology is the best offered plan: the bloodstream isolate and lumbar disc/endplate pattern support one diagnosis, while the separate destructive pedicle/vertebral lesion with a solid mass remains insufficiently explained.

Two consequential interpretations are required: deciding where bloodstream microbiology is sufficiently concordant, then deciding which separate lesion still requires tissue. Sampling L3-L4 and treating both sites empirically are credible different errors.
The explanation correctly does not equate preserved discs with proof of tumor or exclusion of infection. It preserves the uncertainty that makes culture plus histology appropriate.

The shared continuing treatment prevents a false choice between biopsy and treating bacteremia. Hemodynamic and neurological stability support the diagnostic framing. Both sites and the preceding microbiology are restated, so the case is independent of earlier spinal nodes.

Diagnostic anchoring, tissue diagnosis of a discordant destructive lesion and concordant S. aureus spinal infection are valuable, testable principles. The exact two-site scenario is a stretch application, not a claim of documented ABSITE frequency.
suggestions: Preserve the site-specific uncertainty and continuing bacteremia treatment in all options.
Optional clarity: phrase the surveillance option as deferring biopsy with interval imaging, since all plans already continue antimicrobial treatment. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.

title: New neurological deficit during treatment of lumbar infection

cues.phrase: Ankle movement and perineal sensation are reduced, and the patient newly cannot empty the bladder
cues.why: This is a classic urgent spinal-neural pattern. It is necessary safety information, but the current options turn it into direct MRI recognition rather than a difficult second decision.

cues.phrase: a new neurological change has triggered urgent spine-team assessment
cues.why: The update has already resolved escalation and the responsible specialty; the learner only selects the familiar first imaging modality.

fairness: Urgent contrast lumbar MRI alongside specialist assessment is the clear best offered investigation. Falling fever and CRP do not exclude a new compressive or epidural problem.
No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified. The explanation correctly does not claim that a specific mechanism or operation has already been established.

Deleting the improving fever/CRP row leaves exactly the same urgent MRI answer. Thus treatment-response discordance is background, not a necessary second inference. CT is a weaker modality and electrodiagnosis an inappropriate first response to this acute pattern.

The singleton restates treatment for lumbar infection, prior normal function and the new findings. No earlier MRI result or companion answer is needed. This is a high-yield emergency-recognition objective.
suggestions: Seek explicit acceptance as an easy safety-recognition item, or author a separate supported decision after the urgent syndrome has been recognized.
Keep perineal sensory loss, bladder dysfunction and progression. Do not manufacture difficulty by hiding red flags or suggesting an unsafe wait for electrodiagnosis.
If retaining a two-step claim, make an actual supplied finding determine a credible competing next action rather than merely adding reassuring inflammatory trends that cannot change the answer.

title: Foot-drop localization despite pre-existing lumbar narrowing

cues.why: This named omission favors an electrodiagnostic option, but it does not uniquely identify the key because both fibular and tibial study options remain. The motor map still has to be interpreted. This is a nonblocking cue, not a sufficient nonmedical answer shortcut.

fairness: Fibular nerve conduction and needle EMG is the best offered investigation: dorsiflexion/eversion weakness with preserved inversion and hip abduction favors a fibular distribution over assigning causation to the old foraminal image.
Localization changes the study choice before a lumbar intervention is considered. Repeat spine imaging is a plausible anchoring error; a tibial-directed study mismatches the principal deficit.

No confident clinical inaccuracy is identified if 'needle EMG' denotes an appropriate differential localization examination. The feedback should not imply that testing only fibular-innervated muscles definitively excludes a root lesion, or that an old image proves incidental disease.
All relevant postoperative context, examination and prior imaging are restated in the singleton. Peripheral-versus-root localization of foot drop is a high-yield application.
suggestions: Optional cue reduction: remove the named electrodiagnostic omission while preserving the old image and current motor map.

Clarify in feedback that a differential needle examination may sample appropriate nonfibular muscles; retain the distinction between a favored localization and a proven operative mechanism. Editorial PASS is not clinical approval.
